speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: asked the Minister for Home Affairs (a) what is the progress of efforts to uplift the private security industry, in terms of its capacity to complement law enforcement and the career prospects for private security personnel; (b) what are the main challenges in uplifting the private security industry; and (c) how does the Government intend to enforce the enhanced regime in the Private Security Industry (Conduct) Regulations effective January 2019, taking into account the diverse profile of security personnel currently in the industry.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The private security industry is an important partner in our efforts to keep Singapore safe and secure.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The ITM aims to shift the industry away from its current manpower-intensive service model, to one that integrates skilled manpower and technology to deliver higher quality security services.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We want to achieve outcomes of high performing security agencies, more meaningful and better-paying jobs for security officers, and also better security for Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: On the demand side, to encourage buyers to adopt outcome-based contracts which integrate manpower and technology, we have launched a tailored guide for the industry, as well as a training course for procurement officers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: On the technology front, the Infocomm Media and Development Authority and the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) launched the Security Industry Digital Plan in July 2018 to provide security agencies a step-by-step guide on adopting digital technology.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Funding is available for security small and medium enterprises to adopt pre-approved digital solutions under the Productivity Solutions Grant.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: To uplift security officers and improve the attractiveness of the industry, the Progressive Wage Model (PWM) for the industry was enhanced in November 2018, to place stronger emphasis on skills and competencies.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: To open new opportunities to experienced officers, a new Specialist Diploma in Security Consultancy by Temasek Polytechnic will commence in April this year.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: MHA has also reviewed our regulations to support the security ITM.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For security agencies, the annual Security Agencies Grading Exercise was reviewed in 2018 to give greater weight to technology adoption and training.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Security officers, too, have an important part to play in the industry’s transformation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: As part of efforts to enhance the professionalism of the industry, MHA has made certain Code of Conduct breaches that pose a risk to public safety and security compoundable offences under the Private Security Industry Regulations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Our aim is not a punitive regime, but to deter and take targeted action to address unprofessional behaviour, such as sleeping or consuming alcohol on the job, as this may lead to security lapses.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: First time offenders will generally be given warnings, as has been the practice previously.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: However, the Police Licensing and Regulatory Department now has the flexibility to impose a composition fine if a security officer repeatedly or egregiously breaches the Code of Conduct, whereas previously it only had the more severe options of suspending or revoking his licence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Only in the most severe or recalcitrant cases would penalties, such as licence suspension or revocation, and prosecution be considered.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The first is, in her answer, she mentioned – and I think it is welcomed – that the exemption given to private security companies are not to pay overtime or, rather, to require the officers to work overtime is going to be removed progressively in the coming years.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But my question is whether there is also a move towards better working conditions in terms of shorter shifts, for example, instead of the 12-hour shift, to move to an eight-hour shift, because that would be important for the quality of the service provided.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The second question is comparison of the regime now for the private security versus the Police.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We do know that for the Police, for similar conduct breaches, such as sleeping or being absent without official leave, there is the option of departmental action, meaning that there could be a reprimand or a reduction in rank, and the person would still continue in service.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, I would like to ask for the private security industry, maybe the Senior Parliamentary Secretary can elaborate on the middle-road approaches before we actually go to prosecuting or citing the person for an offence under the regulations, which are effective this month.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My final question is that, under the new conduct regulations, there is one sub-paragraph which says that it would be an offence for a private security officer not to respond promptly to any request for assistance by a person who has been injured or suffered loss on the premises.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Now, given that, in that sense, the baseline for entry and the training level for private security officers on the whole is not very rigorous, what is expected of the officer to comply with this section of responding promptly to a request for assistance?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Are they required to intervene, prevent injury and so on?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: So, with the removal of the overtime exemption, we hope to remove this exemption that was given to security agencies and bring it down to 72 hours or less.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Actually, employees as well as the security agencies do not have to wait till January 2021.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: They are encouraged to move on to these new working hours as soon as practically possible, and also to ensure that their wages are protected with the PWM that I had talked about earlier.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: On the second point, already currently in the private security landscape where the security officer was seen to be sleeping on the job or consuming alcohol on the job, which is unprofessional conduct, some of the security agencies are already taking measures, such as the docking of pay, for instance, of the security officer.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: So, even with the new code of conduct amendments, which move some of the code of conduct breaches over to the regulations, the Police and the authorities will actually take a very calibrated approach, a very targeted one.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: So, we will look at the actual egregiousness of the offence that was committed, and we will look at the range of penalties that are available.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I think my answer to that second part actually also answers the third question that the Member had.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Speaker, just to follow up with two other questions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: First is whether the Senior Parliamentary Secretary can specifically confirm or otherwise about whether there is a move to move to shorter shift hours for security officers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: That means, currently, it is quite common to have 12-hour shifts, and whether there is actually a move to try to go into eight-hour shifts.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Last of all, related to the issue of the requirement to respond promptly to request for assistance, I just like to highlight that you do have deployment situations where a security officer may be quite alone in the guard post.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: He is supposed to be there to man and record entrance and so on.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: And if somebody runs to him to say that he needs help and so on, what is expected of that person?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Is the person expected to leave the post to attend to the situation or is it all right for him to just try to call for help?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Maybe the Senior Parliamentary Secretary can elaborate on that.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: On that point, the assessment has to be made as to how big a security lapse it could be if the security officer were to leave his position.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: So, the authorities will take a case-by-case approach.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: As I mentioned, they will look at the action that has been taken.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: They will look at the potential penalties, there is a range of options.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: And as I mentioned, the authorities will actually take a very calibrated and targeted approach.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Actually, the new penalties now allow for them to do so.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: So, if there were any transgressions, they will look at the offence and see whether or not it warrants a lower amount of fine.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: And whether or not they actually implemented that will depend on how serious the security transgression was, and they will definitely look at the circumstances of the case.
